sections.h2: Does Tennessee still have an inheritance or estate tax?
sections.html:
Tennessee's inheritance tax ended with deaths in 2016. The Department of Revenue states that the tax is no longer imposed after December 31, 2015 and tells filers not to submit a return for any decedent whose date of death falls in 2016 or later.

While it lasted, the tax applied to the part of an estate's value above an exemption for the year of death. The net estate was the fair market value of all assets less deductions such as property passing to a surviving spouse, debts and administrative expenses, and the executor, administrator or trustee paid it out of the estate. Heirs selling a Tennessee house today do not deal with that filing. The federal estate tax is the one that can still reach a large estate.

sections.h2: When does the federal estate tax apply to a Tennessee estate?
sections.html:
It applies only when the estate is large. The IRS reports that the Working Families Tax Cuts law, Public Law 119-21 signed July 4, 2025, raised the basic exclusion amount to $15,000,000 for 2026. The table shows how the figure has moved for recent years of death.

Year of deathFederal basic exclusion amount
2023$12,920,000
2024$13,610,000
2025$13,990,000
2026$15,000,000

Source: IRS, What's new, estate and gift tax. A typical Tennessee family home sits far below these amounts, so most heirs never file a Form 706. Add up the house, bank accounts, retirement accounts and life insurance owned by the decedent before assuming no return is needed.

sections.h2: Can a surviving spouse use the unused federal exclusion?
sections.html:
Yes. For decedents dying after January 1, 2011, the estate may elect to pass the decedent's unused exclusion to the surviving spouse. The election is made on a timely filed estate tax return, which means a Form 706 can be worth filing even when no tax is due.

The IRS also notes that simplified valuation rules apply for estates that would not otherwise need to file. A Tennessee widow or widower who expects to sell the family house and keep a large investment portfolio should ask the estate's attorney whether to make this election before the filing deadline passes.

sections.h2: What tax value do heirs use when they sell an inherited house?
sections.html:
The date-of-death value generally becomes the heir's basis. IRS Publication 551 says inherited property takes the fair market value at the date of death, or the alternate valuation date when the executor selected it. A house that was worth $240,000 at death and sells for $245,000 produces a $5,000 gain for federal purposes, whatever the decedent paid decades earlier.

  • When a federal estate tax return was required, the executor provides each beneficiary a Schedule A (Form 8971) with the estate tax value.
  • The IRS issued final regulations on September 16, 2024 on consistent basis reporting between an estate and the person acquiring property from a decedent.
  • An estate that is not required to file a return should not send Form 8971, the IRS warns, because doing so can cause unnecessary correspondence.

For an estate below the filing threshold, order a date-of-death appraisal from a licensed appraiser and keep it with the estate papers.

sections.h2: What does the executor pay when the Tennessee house is deeded to a buyer?
sections.html:
The buyer, as grantee, pays the realty transfer tax. The Department of Revenue's recordation tax page says the county register of deeds collects it, and the rate page lists $0.37 per $100 of purchase price. On a $180,000 estate sale the figure is $666.

Property tax runs on its own track. The county assessor appraises the property, the county commission and city governing bodies set rates, and the county trustee collects the bill, according to the Comptroller's assessment and taxation overview. Ask the county trustee for the current balance on the parcel before the closing date and give that figure to the title company.

sections.h2: How does the county value an inherited house for property tax?
sections.html:
Residential property is assessed at 25 percent of appraised value, so a home appraised at $100,000 carries an assessed value of $25,000. Appraisals are reset in periodic reappraisal programs on a 6, 5 or 4 year cycle, and between those programs the value generally stays put unless the property changes.

  • Valid grounds for an appeal are a value that is too high, another owner's value that is too low, or the wrong classification.
  • The tax amount is not a valid basis for appeal.
  • The steps run from an informal talk with the assessor to the County Board of Equalization, which meets beginning June 1, then the State Board of Equalization and Chancery Court.

An heir who inherits an older house that was appraised years ago can expect the appraisal to change at the next reappraisal.

sections.h2: What if a parent gave the house to a child shortly before dying?
sections.html:
The basis rule changes in one narrow case. Publication 551 says the date-of-death value does not apply to appreciated property you or your spouse gave to the decedent within one year before the decedent's death. If the person later left it back to you, your basis is the decedent's adjusted basis just before death, not the market value.

That rule matters for Tennessee families who retitle a house for care or Medicaid planning and then inherit it back. Appreciated property means property whose market value on the day it was given was higher than the giver's adjusted basis. Talk with the estate's attorney before any retitling so the tax effect is known ahead of time.

sections.h2: Which papers should heirs gather before listing the house?
sections.html:
A complete folder makes the closing smoother and supports the basis you report later. Collect these items before the house goes on the market.

  • The death certificate and the court order or letters naming the person who may sign the deed.
  • The date-of-death appraisal or the Schedule A (Form 8971) if the estate filed a Form 706.
  • The most recent property tax bill and a balance from the county trustee.
  • Receipts for repairs, roof work or additions that the decedent paid for, which the IRS treats as basis improvements.
  • Any mortgage payoff statement from the lender.

Topic no. 409 reminds sellers who owe tax on a gain that estimated tax payments may be required, so ask the preparer about the due dates once an accepted offer exists.

sections.h2: Does a Tennessee estate sale trigger any other tax step?
sections.html:
Two small items come up. The IRS user fee for an estate tax closing letter, Letter 627, rose from $56 to $76 effective October 26, 2026, which matters only to estates that file a Form 706. The annual gift tax exclusion is $19,000 per recipient for 2026, relevant if a parent was moving ownership of the house to children before death.

For the court side of the estate, ask the court clerk in the county where the decedent lived which office handles letters of administration or the probate of a will. That clerk can tell you what the court must approve before a sale and how long recording will take.

faqs.q: Does Tennessee have an inheritance tax in 2026?
faqs.a: No. The Department of Revenue says the inheritance tax is no longer imposed after December 31, 2015, and no return should be filed for deaths in 2016 or later.

faqs.q: What is the federal estate tax exemption for 2026?
faqs.a: It is $15,000,000 per person, set by Public Law 119-21 for deaths in calendar year 2026. A surviving spouse can add the decedent's unused amount by electing on a timely filed return.

faqs.q: What basis do heirs get on an inherited house?
faqs.a: Generally the fair market value on the date of death, or the alternate valuation date if the executor used it. That value is measured against the sale price to find any gain.

faqs.q: Who pays the transfer tax when an estate sells a house?
faqs.a: The grantee, meaning the buyer, pays the realty transfer tax to the register of deeds. The rate is $0.37 per $100 of purchase price.

faqs.q: Can heirs appeal the county's value of an inherited house?
faqs.a: Yes, if the value is too high, another owner's value is too low, or the property is misclassified. Start with the county assessor, then the County Board of Equalization, which meets beginning June 1.
